Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
I fully understand the philosophy and meaning of the "desperate
rulings" that allow players without any "reasonable chances" of
getting any VPs to do everything they want, including crazy crosstable
actions and even self-ousting. Nobody likes just to sit at the table
and wait until somebody ousts him. But, IMHO, the current solution
generates more problems than solves, and it must be changed as soon as
possible.
Let's imagine that there are three remaining players at the table:
Alex, Bob and Claire, sitting in the listed order. Alex is playing a
very good rush deck, so all minions of Bob and Claire are lying
bloodless in their torpors. Who can argue that Alex doesn't really
DESERVE to get a GW? He's built a good deck, and played it right, he
rendered all other players helpless and will inevitably oust them
provided there is enough time. But current rules give Claire the right
to self-oust and "steal" the GW from Alex just because she is
helpless! A tournament where even extremely bad and unfortunate
players decide who will be the winner has nothing common to sport and
shouldn't be called "tournament" at all.
Legal self-ousting negatively affects the metagame, making slowly-
ousting rush and intercept decks (which are already quite difficult to
win with) even more weak. Just look at the example above. A rush
player has to torporize vampires of its predator (to avoid being
ousted) and of its prey (to win). He rarely has chances of preventing
self-oustings "just for the revenge". Same about the wall decks: if
your predator feels that he's unable to oust you, he has the "right"
of stealing your GW.
I bet that most players cannot even imagine how ugly can the game
become when somebody abuses the "desperate rulings". Our players are
already accustomed to the threats of self-ousting, usually to make
somebody's grandpredator to help him. What can be more filthy than "Do
what I say or I will self-oust, and your prey will get 6 pool"? What
would you do if some beggar approach you with a knife, threatening to
commit suicide unless you give him money? I guess you'd call the
police. So why such behaviour should be tolerated in
VTES? But even this isn't the most awful behaviour. Believe me or not,
but in one of my games one player said to his grandpredator: "Make a
deal with me to give me GW, or I'll have to self-oust"! And the deal
was really made!!!

My words bring little new thoughts, I know, since many players already
blamed self-ousting. But, IMHO, if we feel that something should be
changed, we have to struggle for it, and eventually our dreams may
come true. Do you remember the anti-PTO discussions? It took several
years until PTO finally got banned, but our humble voices were heard.
Now it's time to defeat the "self-ousting plague".

I've though for the best solution for a while, and my current
suggestion is following:

1. Change the rules of withdrawing from the game to the following:
---------------------------------
9.2. Withdrawing from the game

To withdraw from the game, you must announce your intent to withdraw
during your untap phase. If you do, all ready vampires you control
must hunt during your next minion phase (even if they have some
blood). Your minions cannot perform any actions directed at other
Methuselahs or cards under their control until your next turn. At end
of your turn, burn all vampires in torpor you control.

For the withdrawal to succeed, none of your vampires should get into
torpor from the withdrawal announcement till your next turn. If you
successfully withdraw, you receive 0.5 victory points to add to any
victory points you have already gained. Your predator gets 0.5 victory
points and 3 pool for your withdrawal.
---------------------------------

2. Change the PTW philosophy to the following:

As long as each player now has the option to withdraw from the game,
there is always a chance of getting 0.5 VP even without the time
limit, and the chance is greater than zero. Self-ousting, as well as
insane behaviour leading to zero VPs, is thereby a clear violation of
PTW, since the player deliberately decreases his "expected outcome"
from the game. If some player feels that he has no reasonable chances
of getting at least 1 VP, he should try to withdraw. Not "avenge the
enemies", not "help his friends to win", just withdraw.

IMHO, the suggested change solves all problems. No player will be
forced to hopelessly wait until somebody ousts him: if he tries to
withdraw, his fate will usually be decided in one turn. Other players
have many ways to prevent him from withdrawing: intercept decks can
block his hunts and torporize somebody, rush decks can rush and
torporize, while bleed and voting decks can just oust him. But look,
if you had no ready vampires, then the only way to prevent you from
withdrawing is ousting you in one turn! And if somebody torporizes
your last vampire to prevent withdrawal, this makes the next attempt
much easier :)

Sure. How was it *kept*, though? Once the player in question has the
two VP that are sitting between him and his grandpredator, and the
grandpredator has his prey's VP, it's a 2P game and the deal is off,
and the grandpredator can win 3-2. If you deal yourself into a losing
position because it's the best option you have of getting VP's, then

as something else, that's different.

And creates many more, particularly by nerfing the very torpor-heavy
decks you're claiming you want to make these changes to support.

Allowing a player in a non-lost position to follow through on such a

Non-sequitur. Suicide is illegal (here in the states, anyway).

deal made a very bad play.

I had a lot of sleepless nights thanks to this problem. What I figured
out is that if everyone would do the following, then there would be no

and "teaching" them. Always remember that v:tes is a GAME!

I think that's the point that many people get stuck on. Every action
or inaction doesn't actually feel as crazy as any other. The lost-
position player had previously been non-lost, and had spent the last
100 minutes trying to oust his/her prey and stay alive. Then, once
the player is in a lost position, he or she suddenly can not stay
alive, not try to oust his/her prey, and instead self-oust or go cross-
table.

Such actions feel more crazy than the other actions, because they are
such a divergence from the previous play style.

In real life, a crazy person is someone who acts unexpectedly and
unpredictably. Trying to stay alive and trying to oust one's prey is
predictable and not crazy. Doing anything else is "crazy."

To be clear, I think that the current rules are good and shouldn't be
changed, and I don't share Ector's view that there is a problem.

The rules don't require a 0% chance. The rules require a "reasonable"
chance. "Reasonable" is defined by the judge, and can vary from judge
to judge. Also, "reasonable" includes weighted averages, so you might
have these choices:
a) 1% chance 5 VP and a GW, 99% chance 0 VPs.
b) 99% chance 2 VPs (and someone else gets GW), 1% chance 0 VPs.

Many judges would rule that b is also "reasonable", and a player would
be free to pick either course of action.

usually expects it.

A few months ago, there was a very long thread discussing a similar
topic. In this thread LSJ confirmed to me that once you have no
chance of gaining additional VPs, you are free to play arbritrarily,
and it is technically sportsmanlike. That means that you can help
your friend and hurt your enemy based completely on your out-of-game
feelings for them as long as you have decided that you cannot gain any
more VPs.

After learning this, I was really turned off by the game. LSJ has
steadfastly refused to give guidance on how to act in these "no-more
VPs" situations, and I have seen the posts of other top VTES players
who believe there should be no defined way to act in "hopeless"
situations. I've read things like "Self-ousting is just another way
to earn your maximum 0 VPs." and "Why punish a stealth-bleeder? That
is arbitrary."

Like Martin I spent some "sleepless nights" thinking about this issue.
I tried to think of a way to act non-arbitrarily when I've reached a
hopeless situation in a game. In my opinion, and it is only an
opinion, arbitrary play comes down to "kingmaking" or "retaliation",
and it is unsportmanslike.

My solution was to focus on tournament points when I can no longer
earn additional VPs. I know that tournament points are only for
tournaments, but I think that they could easily be part of the scoring
of casual games as well. To determine tournament points, you have to
rank the players in a game. If a player can no longer earn more VPs,
he can still act non-abitrarily to try to ensure that as few other
players are ranked above him as possible.

It is an easy system of "ethics" for players in "hopeless" situations.
It's not necessarily pretty - for example, helping an aggressive
predator sweep the table might be the only way for a player to ensure
maximum tournament points. It is also easy to misjudge when things
are hopeless.

If the official rules made tournament points part of the scoring for
casual games, and if the rules said you have to play to maximize your
tournament points after you have maximized your victory points, I
think it would make the game more enjoyable and clear up a lot of
questions about what constitutes sportmanslike play.

It's a perfectly reasonable thing to do, depending on your deck. Having
your prey put pressure on his prey is typically a good thing for most
decks. This is, in fact, the reason that most naive rush decks fail -
they obliterate their prey, oust him via bleeds, and then find
themselves up against their grand-prey who's had almost no pressure on
them all game. In general, this is not a good situation to find
yourself in. (There's the reverse problem too, and often the next step
in a player's evolution of rush decks - going from a) tunnel vision on
prey to b) rushing everyone to try to excessively control the table.)

It's perfectly reasonable to, for example, go about ousting your prey
while a copy of Pentex Subversion keeps that one vampire from blocking
you. I can certainly say that I've seen many poor rush decks that would
be better taking advantage of such a play.

You'll also find that a number of strong players advocate not
demolishing your prey immediately, even if you can, for this reason.
When your prey is down to six pool but has put a couple of bleeds on
your grand-prey, it's perfectly reasonable to then demolish their last
one or two minions (with or without Fame) and bleed them out. If they
have a reasonable buffer of pool (such that it will take you a while to
oust them with bleeds), it may also be to your advantage to keep one out
so that you can try to pull Fame and play it on them immediately.

Obviously, this won't be the right play in all games, but merely to
dismiss potentially good play as "really funny" shows a lack of
understanding of the game.

Note that it is not a rule inclusion. There is no "self-oust" rule.
Self-ousting is simply one example of how the rules on transfers (or
on paying card costs and/or effect costs) can affect the game.

That is, self-ousting is a natural consequence of the basic rules of
the game, and continues to exist because of the absence of a rule
banning it.

Fun factor aside, an(other) reason a rule prohibiting self-ousting has
not been added to the game is because such a rule would either be
unteneble or be so watered down as to have no impact (much like one of
the reasons "no VP deals" has not been added to the ruleset).

That is, coming up with a concrete, loophole-free, devious-Methuselah-
proof statement of a "no self-ousting" rule isn't possible (or at
least, no one has ever produced such a wording) except in emasculated
forms like "cannot spend once's last pool on transfers which
simultaneously go too far (prevent "legitimate" play as described in
this thread already) and have next to no impact (by still allowing a
myriad of easy-to-accomplish ways to self-oust).

Surely, it's impossible to prohibit "0VP behaviour" once it's obvious
that the player has no chances of getting even 0.5 VP. That is the
reason of my withdrawal rule. Give the players a way of getting 0.5
VPs, even in a desperate situation, and then you can force them to
play for these 0.5.

Let me summarize the pros and cons of the current situation compared
to proposed rules changing (in my point of view, of course):

1). The "0VP behaviour" enables even almost-cheating thinks like
attacking crosstable players (even players completely not responsible
for the desperate situation) just to help somebody's friends. And the
rules don't prohibit this, which is obviously bad for the game.
2). The "0VP behaviour" drastically differs from the usual behaviour
of VTES players, as all VTES players are trying to get more VPs than
they currently have, and they're trying to avoid being ousted. Having
one player pursuing different goals from the goals of other players is
definitely bad for the game.
3). The announcement of "desperate situation" can be made at any time
which makes it completely sudden and doesn't allow other players to
react. For instance, if my last action was blocked and my acting
vampire got into torpor, I may decide that my situation became
desperate and immediately self-oust. My withdrawal suggestion at least
gives the other players a turn, which is obviously better.
4). The proposed withdrawal can be interrupted by the other players,
the self-ousting cannot. No chance of interaction is always bad for
the game, you know.
5). The "desperate announcement" causes violent debates almost every
time - each player has his own point of view on whether the situation
is really desperate. Due to the abovementioned reasons, the withdrawal
announcement is much less likely to cause debates and/or these debates
aren't going to be as violent.
6). Prohibiting self-ousting will make the decks that relying on
disabling predator's minions (i.e. rush decks) more attractive, which
is definitely good for the game, as this will increase the variety of
winning strategies.

For me, these 6 things are more than enough to accept the suggested
rules change. And I really don't see any "contra" arguments, besides
the keeping status quo.

Well, at last we have a serious theme to discuss! First of all, let me
present the final version of the new withdrawing rule and thank all
people who helped me to fix it:

----------------------------------------------
9.2. Withdrawing from the game

To withdraw from the game, you must announce your intent to withdraw
during your untap phase. If you do, all ready vampires you control
must hunt during your next minion phase (even if they have some
blood). Your minions cannot perform any actions directed at other
Methuselahs or cards under their control until your next turn. At end
of your turn, burn all vampires in torpor you control.

You cannot attempt to withdraw from the game if you have 2 or more
victory points.
This means you're too close for the victory to withdraw!

For the withdrawal to succeed, none of your minions should leave the
ready region
from the withdrawal announcement till your next turn. If you
successfully withdraw,
you receive 0.5 victory points to add to any victory points you have
already gained.
Your predator gets 0.5 victory points and 3 pool for your withdrawal.
-----------------------------------------------

Now let's see whether my arguments to prove that the new rules would
be better for the game are serious or not. I'd also like to see your
arguments to prove that the current rules are better, if you have
them :)

1). The current rules make Cheating: Collusion much easier and almost
impossible to punish.

Problem: When the player's "desperate" status is approved by a judge,
that player can legally harm crosstable players and perform any
actions, including actions to help his friends/relatives to get better
results. This can be Cheating: Collusion, but no judge has any reasons
of accusing such players, and DQing a player without a prove is very
unlikely.
Solution: The proposed rules never allows players to do everything
they want. If a player tries to perform a suspicious action, he should
always explain to the judge how his behavior is supposed to help him
to get GW or more VPs.
Conclusion: The proposed version is obviously better.

2). The current rules provide too low (by VTES standards) level of
interaction between the leaving player and the other players.

Problem: In many cases, self-ousting happens suddenly, and the other
players have no way of preventing it except for Life Boon.
Solution: The proposed withdrawal rule gives the other players a turn
to react to the withdrawal attempt, if they want to. It also allows
other players to prevent the leaving player from withdrawing using the
standard VTES mechanics that don't require narrow-usage cards. Almost
every deck archetype can try to prevent the withdrawal using its
primary strategy: rush decks can torporize some vampires, intercept
decks can block the hunt and torporize, voting decks can play
Banishment. Still, the withdrawal is quite possible, especially if the
player has enough Combat Ends.
Conclusion: Unlike the current rules, the proposed version provides
the level of interaction that is going to appeal most VTES players,
and thus is better.

3). The current rules are much more likely to generate the
unproductive debates.

Problem: Different people (even different judges) have different
meaning on whether the player's situation is really "desperate" or
not. As long as this decision often leads to radical changes in the
game flow (see 1), and the insuffucient level of interaction during
self-ousting (see 2), players feel that the debating is their only
chance to do something.
Solution: As long as the proposed withdrawing rule deals with problems
1 and 2, the debates are much less likely.
Conclusion: Debates are always bad for the game, so reducing chance of
their appearance and their level is definitely good.

4). The current rules hoses the decks relying on disabling predator's
minions.

Problem: Any deck that tries to disable its predator's minions instead
of defending from their actions finds it very difficult to win, since
every player with the disabled minions can self-oust, forcing it to
deal with the new predator.
Solution: Under the new rules, players with disabled minions can
withdraw, but at least the disabling deck will get one extra turn of
safety. It also gets a chance to prevent withdrawal if the leaving
player has at least one ready minion.
Conclusion: As long as the disabling decks aren't very popular
compared to other deck types, increasing their chances is good for the
game since it increases the variety of "good decks".

ready minions is *really* helpless - compare this to the mentioned

has two distinct advantages compared to the current rules:
a). Everyone can easily evaluate the player's chances of withdrawing,
and everybody knows that killing the last minion would make
withdrawing very easy. This at least allow them to plan their
behaviour ahead. Such planning is currently very difficult, since it's
very difficult to predict whether someone's situation is really lost
(especially if you don't know that player and his deck).
b). Each time somebody torporizes the vampire to prevent withdrawing,
this makes the next withdrawing easier :)

>

> a) "increased interactivity" and b) empowering minion control
> strategies, especially rush combat decks.

No, it doesn't counter the increased interactivity and empowering
minion control strategies. It just tries to keep balance between solid
chances of withdrawal (there is really no need to force desperate
players to play) and solid chances of preventing the withdrawal. Both
are needed for the good game.
Rush decks are gaining a lot. Even if the withdrawing player has no
minions, the withdrawal will take the whole turn while self-ousting
could happen immediately. This provides some chances of ousting your
prey and then getting the 0.5 from the withdrawal. Note that every
deck will initially have some minions, so you can leave your predator
one minion and have two turns: on the first turn, your predator
attempts to withdraw, but you kill his last minion, and the second
attempt will finally succeed - if nobody would oust that player, of
course. What could the rush deck get now? Not even a single turn.
Interactivity also obviously increases, except for the zero-minions
situations. I guess you aren't packing tons of Life Boons, so you
generally can do NOTHING to prevent self-ousting. But you can do a lot
of things to prevent self-ousting if the player has ready minions.
Losing all ready minions doesn't happen at once, and all players are
going to be aware of the consequences. At least nobody can suddenly
self-oust having several ready minions.

> In fact, rush combat would likely suffer tremendously since as soon as
> your prey has no ready minions left, he`ll just withdraw leaving you
> with 0,5 VP. Dunk your predators minions, and he`ll take his
> guaranteed 0,5 over being ousted.

when he should torporize and when he shouldn't. Thus, he can leave his
predator just one minion to torporize it if the predator would try to
withdraw. He can also leave his prey one minion for the same purpose.
Then, one vampire will rush it, while the other will bleed.
Also note that torporizing a vampire and then resquing it still
prevents the withdrawal :)

position is lost or not except for himself and the judge. You don't
get to look at his hand or his library. But everybody knows how much
ready minions he has. Thus, it's far from being "the same".

>

That's the game. You have to spend some resources to gain something,
and you decide whether that "something" is worth the resources or not.
And the other players can thwart your plans.

> Is he going to do that for every other methusalah on the table, if
> necessary?

He decides. That's the game.

> What if he just runs out of rushes or jams on combat cards?

What if any deck just runs out of the needed cards? That's the game.
Nothing is granted.

> What if predator or prey stop bringing out vampires after the first
> one, or refuse to bring out vampires, waiting for an opening, and
> withdrawing when they see it`ll never come.

All this can happen even without my changes. While the player still
has some chances to get VPs, he cannot withdraw. Once he doesn't have
them, he can be ousted.

> What if his grandprey does it afer a vain attempt by the rush player
> to balance the table by rushing crosstable?

Who's to blame, then?

> When people have the option for a guarantted 05. Vp, the will take
> that possiblity into account from the beginning of the game.

The withdrawal is far from guaranteed. Sometimes even very far
(depends on the game situation, of course).

> Not to mention the fact that dunking a vampire, then rescuing him and
> leaving him ready to possibly act again seems to be a bad plan in
> general.

Nobody has to do it - it's a player's choice. That's the game.

Let me point at one important thing. Without the self-ousting, the
player in lost position would have to wait until somebody oust him,
which is bad. With self-ousting, he can leave the game, which is
better. But with my suggestion, he can PLAY the game of withdrawal,
which is far more interesting than just bringing some chaos and
leaving. I'm completely sure that most players would choose to
withdraw instead of self-ousting.

definition is "no reasonable chance of getting VPs", which enables

turn. If a bad player bleeds his prey for 3 pool per turn, and the
prey gains at least 4 per turn, it's pretty obvious that the player

"Worshipping" was just a sarcasm, though quite bitter.
I'm completely aware of all the details of judge's work, since I've
been a judge in various games for more than 10 years, including Magic.
A judge is supposed to know the rules, to maintain the order, to
ensure that newbs aren't deceived or mistreated, etc. etc.
But all games I know follow the two basic principles:
1). The judge should keep his interference minimal. If everything is
OK, no interference is needed at all.
2). The judge should NEVER determine the game outcome, except for the
cases when some player is punished (Game Loss etc).

Obviously, the current "lost position" rulings break both principles.
Every time somebody tries to declare himself "lost", a judge
interference is *required*. And every time the judge actually
determines the outcome of the game. This is too much responsibility
for a mere mortal, even a judge.
Remember, the judge is not a Dungeon Master, and the whole game
universe is not completely in his mind. The result of game has its own
meaning, unlike the result of any combat in the RPG. A Dungeon Master
can revive the dead PCs, a judge cannot reverse the result of a
finished game, even if he would find out that his judgement was
incorrect.

If we look at the rules that makes the game so much more complicated,
it's hard to refrain from asking: what for? What does the game get for
such immense price? Just to let the players to get out of the game
table a few minutes earlier???

Not at all. You keep telling us how V:TES must become more like a
sport, but apparently don't know much about sports.

- In a wide variety of sports, a judge is required to ascertain whether
someone is intentionally cheating in some fashion. For example, in a
team game (soccer, rugby, American football etc.), the referee might
choose a more serious penalty if he believes the particular infraction
was intentional rather than unintentional. Can this mean the judge
changes the results of the game, based on his judgment? Yes. In
rugby, for example, being awarded a penalty (serious) vs a free kick
(less serious) vs a scrum (not very serious) can have a profound
effect on a game.

How is it decided? Judgment. Is this subjective? All the time.
Even impartial TV and radio commentary teams will disagree on whether
a particular infraction deserved a particular penalty or not.

This can go beyond the current game. If a particular player is
punished with a high severity (such as yellow and red cards in
soccer), this can prevent them playing in future games, which will
affect the outcome there too. The threshold between a foul and a
yellow card, and a yellow card and a red card, is often subjective.
Certainly, the exact boundaries are murky.

- In a number of one-on-one sports, it is absolutely the role of the
referee to determine that both players are being aggressive. That is,
that both players are trying to win in the spirit of the game. I've
certainly seen a number of one-on-one combative sports where a referee
is encouraged to intervene if one player is being excessively
defensive and appears to only be playing for a draw.

How do they determine that? Judgment. Can it affect the outcome of
the match? Absolutely.

- In some team-sports, judges are empowered to see if the team manager
is playing to win. In football (soccer), for example, the rules of
the Premier League state that clubs should "field a full strength
team", and can't just decide to field their second team in a game to
conserve energy and prevent injuries. (See <http://news.bbc.co.uk/spo
rt1/hi/football/eng_prem/8408337.stm> as one example.)

However, the threshold is subjective - a team might have several good
players competing for a sport, and choosing the inexperienced newbie
over the trusted oldbie every now and then is going to make sense for
the team. Trying out new permutations will make sense, to see if you
can improve your outcomes. So the threshold is subjective. Can this
determine the outcome of a game? Usually, the investigation is
retrospective, but the relevant governing bodies can have quite
extensive powers.

The role of judges in many sports is far beyond robotic decision. So,
congratulations, V:TES is just like a real sport in this regard.
Shouldn't you be happy?

Political action
